content: Oritavancin is indicated for the treatment of acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections. It is administered as a single 1200 mg intravenous dose. There are two available oritavancin products, Orbactiv and Kimyrsa, which differ in dose strengths, infusion durations, reconstitution and dilution instructions, and compatible diluents. The safety and efficacy of oritavancin in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. Coadministration of oritavancin with the cholera vaccine should be avoided due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Systemic antibiotics, including oritavancin, may be active against the vaccine strain, reducing the vaccine's efficacy. Cholera vaccine should not be administered to patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. Oritavancin may decrease the effects of oral microbiota products, which contain bacterial spores, through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Antibacterial agents may reduce the efficacy of these products if coadministered. It is recommended to complete antibiotic regimens 2-4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Oritavancin interacts with several drugs by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme metabolism, particularly CYP450 enzymes. It is a weak inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 and a weak inhibitor of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19. These interactions may alter the levels or effects of drugs metabolized by these enzymes, such as carbamazepine, clonidine, disopyramide, ethosuximide, flecainide, fosphenytoin, phenobarbital, phenytoin, primidone, quinidine, quinine, sirolimus, tacrolimus, valproic acid, and cyclosporine. Caution and close monitoring are advised when coadministering oritavancin with these drugs, especially those with a narrow therapeutic index. Oritavancin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to oritavancin products or other glycopeptides (e.g., dalbavancin, telavancin, vancomycin). Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. If acute hypersensitivity occurs, the infusion should be discontinued, and patients with known glycopeptide hypersensitivity should be closely monitored. Infusion-related reactions resembling Red-Man Syndrome (e.g., flushing of the upper body, urticaria, pruritus, rash) have been reported. Slowing the infusion rate or interrupting the infusion may alleviate these reactions. Other infusion reactions, such as chest pain, back pain, chills, and tremor, have also been observed. These reactions may resolve upon stopping or slowing the infusion. The safety and effectiveness of administering more than one dose during a single course of therapy have not been established. In clinical trials, more cases of osteomyelitis were reported with oritavancin compared to vancomycin. If osteomyelitis is suspected, appropriate alternative antibacterial therapy should be initiated. To reduce the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain the effectiveness of oritavancin, it should only be used to treat infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. There are no available data on the use of oritavancin in pregnant women to evaluate the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. Oritavancin has been detected in the breast milk of rats, suggesting it may be present in human milk. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be considered alongside the mother's clinical need for oritavancin and any potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. Oritavancin may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as blood clotting tests (e.g., PT/INR/aPTT), potentially causing false test results. Patients should inform their healthcare providers about their use of oritavancin before undergoing lab tests. This medication may rarely cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile). This condition may occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Prolonged or repeated use of oritavancin may result in oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies or medical history before using oritavancin. Live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine) may not work well during oritavancin treatment. During pregnancy, oritavancin should only be used when clearly needed. It is unknown if this drug passes into breast milk. Patients should keep a list of all medications and share it with their healthcare provider to avoid potential drug interactions. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention.
